newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hashimoto calls for annual Japan-ASEAN summits.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto calls for annual Japan-ASEAN summits.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Monday called for summit meetings at least once a year with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to deepen ties with the increasingly influential region.
"I hope we will be able to meet at least once a year, be it formal or informal," he told a news conference near the end of a five-nation tour of Southeast Asia.
Hashimoto denied there had been a cool reception to his proposal during visits to Brunei, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam and Singapore, all members of ASEAN along with the Philippines and Thailand.
"I don't think there was any leader who showed a passive or negative response to the idea," he said.
A Japanese official, who asked not to be identified, said earlier that Indonesian President Suharto would propose regular summits between Japan and ASEAN leaders when they met in December.
"Suharto was the most supportive. He told us he would propose an intensification of top leaders' contacts in December," the official told reporters.

Hashimoto said he had made the tour despite the crisis in Peru, where Marxist rebels have been holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence for nearly four weeks, because he believed in the need to push for better ties with ASEAN.

"The decision was a difficult one for me. I am truly glad now that I made the trip," he said. "I am convinced that through this trip we have fully cemented relations and we have fully attained the aim of deepening relations between Japan and ASEAN."
Japan already participates in annual meetings with ASEAN, along with the United States and the European Union, at the foreign minister level.
ASEAN, home to some of the world's fastest-growing economies and increasingly courted on the diplomatic stage, has not held regular summits with leaders from outside the organisation.
About 16 percent of Japan's total trade is with ASEAN, and Japanese firms are big investors in the region.
But Hashimoto's trip was aimed at moving ties with ASEAN beyond the economic level.

He was scheduled to make a major policy speech in Singapore on Tuesday before returning to Tokyo, but so far he has offered no real details of how Japan's ties with ASEAN would be taken to a new stage.

He avoided a direct answer when asked if Japan saw a resurgent China as a present or potential threat to stability in Asia that required such enhanced ties, although he admitted there were differences between the two countries.
"We should never allow such differences to undermine Sino-Japanese relations," he said. "We believe the international community should make efforts to engage China as a partner.
He was much blunter on Burma, which is due to join ASEAN along with Laos and Cambodia in the near future, a move he said Japan supported.

"This means Burma will be brought into the international community and be subject to the international rules of the game," Hashimoto said. Burma is ruled by a military-led government which has been cracking down on democracy activists.
